passage:
Monday. Joseph used to be the first to answer in physics. Today, when Ma'am asked him, he just shrugged. Reena, his sister, noticed he left the dinner table early, his phone face down.
Thursday. Joseph ate lunch alone behind the library. At home, Reena heard him moving around at two in the morning, the light under his door still on. When she knocked, he said, "Go to sleep, I'm fine."
The next Monday. Joseph didn't want to go to school. "Headache." Reena sat on his bed. "You can tell me." He stared at the ceiling. "There's no point. Nobody would believe me anyway." His voice cracked on the last word. Reena didn't leave. She stayed right there.

qa.q: Where did Joseph eat lunch on Thursday?
qa.a: He ate lunch alone behind the library.

qa.q: What does Joseph's line "Nobody would believe me anyway" suggest he feels?
qa.a: He feels isolated and hopeless, believing no one would believe or help him, which hurts even more than the bullying itself.

qa.q: What turning point is available now, and how could Reena use it?
qa.a: Joseph has almost opened up; Reena can stay calm, tell him she believes him and it is not his fault, and help him tell their parents or a school counsellor today. 🤍

qa.q: What is it like for Reena watching her brother over these days?
qa.a: She is likely worried and helpless as she sees him go quiet, lose sleep and say he is fine when he clearly is not.

grounding: It shows a teen boy going silent in class, eating alone, sleeping badly and saying he is fine, believing nobody would believe or help him.

passage: Minakshi, sit with your Sharmila Nani. You asked why I always ask your cousins how school really is. When your Ravi mama was fifteen, he stopped talking at dinner. I thought it was the age. He ate in his room and his light was on until three. When I asked, he said, "I'm fine, Amma." Always fine. I believed him because I wanted to. Months later his friend's mother told me the boys had been cornering him every day, and posting things. I asked Ravi why he never told me. He said, "I thought you'd say ignore them. I thought nobody could help." That sentence still sits in my chest. So I ask, beta. And I listen.

qa.q: Until what time was Ravi's light on?
qa.a: His light was on until three.

qa.q: Why didn't Ravi tell his mother about the bullying?
qa.a: He believed nobody could help and thought she would just say ignore them, so he felt alone with it.

qa.q: What could Sharmila Nani have done differently at that stage?
qa.a: When Ravi withdrew and kept saying "I'm fine," she could have gently kept asking, told him she would believe and help him, and contacted the school.

qa.q: How does Sharmila Nani still feel about that time?
qa.a: She still carries regret; Ravi's words still sit in her chest, which is why she now asks her grandchildren and listens.

grounding: It illustrates a teenage boy withdrawing, eating alone, sleeping badly and saying he is fine, believing no one could help him.

passage:
Looking back, I can see exactly when I disappeared.

It was after the edited photos went round in Class 9. I stopped answering in class, even when I knew the answer. I ate lunch in the library, alone. At night I lay awake replaying every laugh.

My sister Ankita kept asking, "Lokesh, what's wrong?" I kept saying, "Nothing. I'm fine." I said it so many times I almost believed it.

The worst part wasn't the photos. It was being sure nobody would believe me, or that telling would just make it bigger.

One night Ankita came into my room, sat on the floor and said, "I saw the photos. I'm not leaving till you talk." I cried for the first time in weeks. She woke our parents that same night, and Papa sat with us until two, promising we'd go to the principal together in the morning. We did.

qa.q: Where did Lokesh eat lunch after the photos?
qa.a: In the library, alone.

qa.q: What did Lokesh feel most deeply during that time?
qa.a: Lokesh felt lonely and hopeless, sure that nobody would believe or help, which hurt more than the photos.

qa.q: What did Ankita do that broke the isolation?
qa.a: She refused to accept "I'm fine", sat with Lokesh until the truth came out, and woke their parents that same night.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt hearing "I'm fine" again and again?
qa.a: She was probably worried and frustrated, sensing something was badly wrong.

grounding: Lokesh withdraws after being bullied, stops speaking in class, eats alone, sleeps badly and says he is fine, until his sister and parents step in the same night.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Thursday

Saurabh used to be one of the first to answer in physics. For three weeks he has not spoken in class. He eats his lunch alone on the back stairs and looks exhausted; he told me he "just isn't sleeping well."

When I asked if something was wrong, he said, "I'm fine, Ma'am." His hands were shaking.

Today Minakshi from his class stayed back and quietly showed me messages from a group chat mocking Saurabh. She said he had stopped replying to everyone, even her.

I found Saurabh at the back stairs at lunch and sat with him. I told him I had seen the messages, that it was not his fault, and that I believed him before he said anything. He cried. I took him to the counsellor, informed the principal, and phoned his father before the end of school.

— Minakshi's class teacher, Mrs Das

qa.q: Where did Saurabh eat his lunch?
qa.a: Alone on the back stairs.

qa.q: What does Saurabh saying "I'm fine" with shaking hands suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he is not fine; he feels hurt, lonely and afraid, perhaps sure no one would believe or help.

qa.q: What did Mrs Das do well?
qa.a: She took Minakshi's evidence seriously, sat with Saurabh, said she believed him and it wasn't his fault, and got the counsellor, principal and his father involved the same day.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt showing the messages to the teacher?
qa.a: She was probably nervous but relieved, worried for Saurabh after he stopped replying even to her.

grounding: A teacher's note shows Saurabh withdrawing, eating alone and saying he is fine, and the teacher acting the same day after a classmate shares evidence.

passage:
Sunday night

Didn't go down for dinner again. Told Ma I had a headache.

A month since Tushar's group made that page about me. I don't talk in class anymore. If I say anything, someone laughs. I eat my tiffin in the chemistry lab where nobody goes.

I can't sleep. I keep checking the page at 2 a.m. to see what they've added.

Ma keeps asking if I'm okay. I keep saying yes. What's the point? If I tell her, she'll go to school, and they'll just say it's a joke, and then it'll be worse. Nobody would believe how bad it is anyway.

Later —

Ma came up with a plate and saw my screen before I could close it. She sat on my bed, read everything, and held my hand. She said, "I believe you. This is not your fault." She called Papa home and they rang my class teacher tonight. Tomorrow we go in together.

— Shankar

qa.q: Where does Shankar eat lunch now?
qa.a: In the chemistry lab where nobody goes.

qa.q: Why does Shankar keep saying he's okay?
qa.a: Shankar feels hopeless and alone, sure that telling would make it worse and that nobody would believe how bad it is.

qa.q: How did Ma respond, and why was it the right response?
qa.a: She read everything, said she believed Shankar and it wasn't Shankar's fault, and with Papa rang the class teacher that same night.

qa.q: How might Ma have felt when she saw the screen?
qa.a: She was probably shocked and heartbroken, but stayed calm and protective.

grounding: Shankar's diary shows him withdrawing, eating alone, sleeping badly and saying he is fine, until his mother sees the page and acts that night.

Naveen: wasn't hungry
Gautam: you ate alone on the stairs. I saw
Naveen: it's fine
Gautam: you haven't said one word in class all week
Naveen: nothing to say
Gautam: is it the video thing? the one they keep sharing?
Naveen: ...
Naveen: every time I walk in someone plays the sound
Naveen: I can't sleep. I keep hearing it
Naveen: don't tell anyone. nobody would believe me anyway, they'd say it's just jokes
Gautam: I believe you. and I'm not keeping this secret, sorry. my dad's right here. can he call your mum now?
Naveen: ...ok
Twenty minutes later Gautam's father was on the phone with Naveen's mother. By eight o'clock she had emailed the class teacher and was sitting beside Naveen on the bed, listening.

qa.q: Why does Naveen keep saying 'it's fine'?
qa.a: Naveen feels ashamed and hopeless, believing nobody would believe it and that it would be brushed off as jokes.

qa.q: What did Gautam do that helped, and why was it right?
qa.a: Gautam said 'I believe you', refused to keep it secret and got a parent to call Naveen's mother that same evening, so an adult could act.

qa.q: What is it like for Gautam to go against Naveen's wish for secrecy?
qa.a: Gautam may feel torn and worried about upsetting a friend, but chooses safety over secrecy because Naveen is clearly suffering.
